name: Socioemotional selectivity theory
statement: Socioemotional selectivity theory holds that shrinking time horizons push emotional goals forward, tilting older adults' attention and memory towards positive over negative material.
meaning: Two claims sit inside one name. The theory is about motivation: when the future looks open, goals about gathering information win, and when it looks short, goals about feeling well in the present take over. Carstensen, Isaacowitz and Charles argue that time perception rather than age does the work, so the same shift should appear in a young person who has been told the future is brief. The positivity effect is the cognitive prediction that follows, and it is measured as an interaction rather than as a preference. Older adults' bias towards positive over negative material is set against younger adults' bias on the same contrast. That arithmetic means the effect can come from older adults leaning positive, from younger adults leaning negative, or from both at once. Reed, Chan and Mikels found both. Pooling 100 studies, older adults carried a positive bias of d = 0.128 and younger adults a negative bias of d = -0.123.

origin.note: The paper that puts the theory's name in a title runs from page 331 to page 338 of volume 7, issue 3. It rated 34 years of transcribed interviews with 28 women and 22 men from the Child Guidance Study and found interaction with acquaintances and close friends declining from early adulthood while emotional closeness with relatives and close friends rose. It is about social networks and says nothing about attention or memory. The full statement of the theory is Carstensen, Isaacowitz and Charles in American Psychologist in 1999, and the memory prediction was tested by Charles, Mather and Carstensen in 2003.

evidence: Charles, Mather and Carstensen ran the founding memory studies in 2003. Study 1 showed 32 images, 16 neutral and 8 each positive and negative, to 144 adults split into three groups of 48 aged 18 to 29, 41 to 53 and 65 to 80. They were told to watch as they would a television, then spent about 15 minutes on questionnaires and cognitive tasks before writing down every image they could recall. The Emotional Valence by Age Group interaction was significant, F(4, 139) = 4.03, p < .001, eta squared = .05. Middle-aged and older adults recalled more positive than negative images while younger adults recalled similar numbers of each. Study 2 gave 32 younger adults aged 19 to 30 and 32 older adults aged 63 to 86 a self-paced run through 78 images, F(2, 61) = 6.19, p < .001, eta squared = .09, and the shape was different: younger adults recalled 13.09 negative against 9.97 positive, while older adults recalled 6.91 negative and 6.13 positive. Barber, Opitz, Martins, Sakaki and Mather tested the motivational mechanism in 2016. They had 77 younger and 76 older adults write about a future holding either six more months of life or a life lasting to 120, then measured the positivity of recall. The limited horizon raised positivity in both age groups, F(1, 149) = 5.17, p = .024, partial eta squared = .03, alongside the usual age effect, F(1, 149) = 10.04, p = .002, partial eta squared = .06.

replication.headline: Across 100 studies the effect is reliable, and it vanishes for older adults in tasks that tell them how to process the material.
replication.detail: Reed, Chan and Mikels pooled 100 studies giving 115 comparisons and 7,129 participants, under a random effects model, from a literature search running to June 2011. The overall positivity effect was d = 0.257, 95% CI [0.165, 0.349], Z = 5.48, p < .001. Within age groups, older adults held a positive bias of d = 0.128, 95% CI [0.042, 0.214], and younger adults a negative bias of d = -0.123, 95% CI [-0.203, -0.043]. The moderators are the finding. Where processing was unconstrained the effect was d = 0.482, 95% CI [0.323, 0.640]; where it was constrained the effect was d = 0.134, 95% CI [0.033, 0.235]. Constrained meant telling participants a memory test was coming, making them rate or judge the stimuli, or steering attention towards or away from valenced material. Under those conditions older adults showed no positive bias at all, d = 0.048, 95% CI [-0.048, 0.144], p = .33, and what remained of the age difference rested on younger adults' negativity. The second moderator is how far apart the two samples were in age. Regressing effect size on the squared difference in mean age gave b = 0.0001, SE = 0.000018, 95% CI [0.000083, 0.000121], Z = 10.32, p < .001, and the slope was steeper in studies without processing constraints, b = 0.00019, than in those with them, b = 0.00004. Three publication-bias tests came out clean: a fail-safe N of 2,913, an Egger intercept of -0.14, t(113) = 0.19, p = .85, and a trim-and-fill estimate of d = 0.43, 95% CI [0.39, 0.48], above the observed value rather than below it. The disagreement is with the earlier meta-analysis. Murphy and Isaacowitz pooled 1,085 older adults from 37 samples and 3,150 younger adults from 86 samples in 2008, found small to medium emotion salience effects in both age groups, and reported few age differences overall. Reed and colleagues answer that roughly 85% of the studies in it had designs that could not test the age by valence interaction, and that its contrasts set positive or negative against neutral rather than positive against negative, a limit Murphy and Isaacowitz state on page 265 of their own paper.

study.cite: Reed, A. E., Chan, L., & Mikels, J. A. (2014). Meta-analysis of the age-related positivity effect: Age differences in preferences for positive over negative information. Psychology and Aging, 29(1), 1-15.

limits: Reed and colleagues name most of the boundaries themselves. Cognitive control could not be tested as a moderator because background ability measures were selected and reported inconsistently across studies, and they call this a key tenet of the account they are defending. Culture could not be tested for want of non-Western samples. Stakes could not be tested because most tasks are trivial, choosing a hypothetical car rather than a life-saving procedure. Every included study is cross-sectional, so nothing in the pooled result shows a change inside one person. Their inclusion rule also admitted studies with no neutral condition, which is why the meta-analysis cannot say whether the age difference comes from more positive processing or less negative. Independence is worth stating: Reed and Carstensen's 2012 review supplied the hypotheses being tested, and the constrained against unconstrained coding was done by the first two authors, agreeing on 92.7% of studies. The search stops at June 2011. No published successor was found in Crossref, PubMed or Europe PMC up to August 2026, and an updated meta-analysis adding social cognition tasks was registered on OSF as dhmfq in June 2018 without a paper attached to it. The clearest single null is Grühn, Smith and Baltes, who tested 72 younger adults aged 18 to 31 and 72 older adults aged 64 to 75 on emotionally toned word lists in 2005 and found no aging bias favouring positive material. Reed and colleagues place that study among those that instruct participants to remember all the information, which is their constrained category.
misreadings: The effect is not older adults remembering happy things more than sad ones. In Charles and colleagues' second study older adults recalled 6.91 negative images and 6.13 positive ones, so the advantage for negative narrowed rather than turned over, and their first study and their second do not even agree on which group shows the tilt. It is not a fact about old age on its own. Part of the age difference in the meta-analysis is younger adults' pull towards negative material, d = -0.123. It is not decline. Reed and colleagues report the effect is clearest when comparing younger and older people with better rather than poorer cognitive control, citing Mather and Knight's 2005 study, which runs against accounts that blame an ageing amygdala. It is not unconditional. Tell older adults that a memory test is coming and their positive bias measures 0.048 with an interval spanning zero. It is not the same claim as the Pollyanna principle or rosy retrospection, which concern which words a language uses most and how one event is rated before, during and after it. And the theory is about perceived time rather than years lived, which is why Barber and colleagues could raise younger adults' recall positivity by asking them to imagine six months left.

sources.text: Carstensen, L. L. (1992). Social and emotional patterns in adulthood: Support for socioemotional selectivity theory. Psychology and Aging, 7(3), 331-338. Read at abstract level via PubMed; no figure beyond the sample composition is quoted from it.

Carstensen, L. L., Isaacowitz, D. M., & Charles, S. T. (1999). Taking time seriously: A theory of socioemotional selectivity. American Psychologist, 54(3), 165-181. Read in full as an author-uploaded copy; the source for the theory's claims about time perception and goal selection.

Charles, S. T., Mather, M., & Carstensen, L. L. (2003). Aging and emotional memory: The forgettable nature of negative images for older adults. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 132(2), 310-324. Read in full; the source for every figure attributed to Study 1 and Study 2.

Reed, A. E., Chan, L., & Mikels, J. A. (2014). Meta-analysis of the age-related positivity effect: Age differences in preferences for positive over negative information. Psychology and Aging, 29(1), 1-15. Closed at the publisher; read in full as an author-hosted copy, which is the source for the pooled estimates, the moderator analyses and the publication-bias tests.

Murphy, N. A., & Isaacowitz, D. M. (2008). Preferences for emotional information in older and younger adults: A meta-analysis of memory and attention tasks. Psychology and Aging, 23(2), 263-286. Read at abstract level only; the page 265 caveat is quoted through Reed, Chan and Mikels' description of it.

Grühn, D., Smith, J., & Baltes, P. B. (2005). No aging bias favoring memory for positive material: Evidence from a heterogeneity-homogeneity list paradigm using emotionally toned words. Psychology and Aging, 20(4), 579-588. Read at abstract level only.

Barber, S. J., Opitz, P. C., Martins, B., Sakaki, M., & Mather, M. (2016). Thinking about a limited future enhances the positivity of younger and older adults' recall: Support for socioemotional selectivity theory. Memory & Cognition, 44(6), 869-882.
Reed, A. E., & Carstensen, L. L. (2012). The theory behind the age-related positivity effect. Frontiers in Psychology, 3, 339. The review that supplied the meta-analysis its hypotheses.
West, J. T. Age-Related Positivity Effect Meta-Analysis. OSF registration dhmfq, registered 27 June 2018, listing one contributor. Registration only; no resulting paper was located.
